lead: A finite automaton is a machine with a fixed set of states. It reads one input symbol at a time and changes state. A DFA allows exactly one move per symbol; an NFA allows several moves and ε-moves. Both recognise the same class, the regular languages. A lexer needs a fast recogniser for token patterns. So we build an NFA from a regular expression, convert it to a DFA, and minimise the DFA.
prereq: You need: regular expressions and transition diagrams from 1.6 and 1.7.

sections.h3: DFA and NFA: the two machines

blocks.text: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is a 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F). Q is a finite set of states. Σ is the input alphabet. δ: Q × Σ → Q is the transition function. q₀ ∈ Q is the start state. F ⊆ Q is the set of accepting states. For every state and every symbol there is exactly one next state. To run a DFA, start at q₀, read the input left to right, and follow δ. Accept the string if the last state is in F.

A nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) is (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) with δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → 2<sup>Q</sup>. The symbol 2<sup>Q</sup> means the set of all subsets of Q. So δ(q, a) is a set of states, not one state. An ε-move changes state without reading a symbol. An NFA accepts a string if some path from q₀ to a state in F spells that string. The NFA may have many paths; the DFA has one.

For a set S of NFA states, ε-closure(S) is every NFA state reachable from a state in S by zero or more ε-moves. For a symbol a, move(S, a) = ⋃<sub>p∈S</sub> δ(p, a). The next subset after reading a is ε-closure(move(S, a)).

sections.h3: Regular expression to NFA, then to DFA

blocks.text: Thompson construction builds an NFA from a regular expression using small pieces. A symbol a becomes two states with one edge labelled a. For R|S, add a new start with ε-edges to the starts of R and S, and ε-edges from their accept states to a new accept state. For RS, connect the accept state of R to the start of S with an ε-edge. For R*, add a new start and accept; ε-edges go from the new start to the start of R and to the new accept, and from the accept of R back to its start and to the new accept.
Subset construction, also called the powerset construction, turns an NFA into a DFA. Each DFA state is a set of NFA states.

items: Compute the start DFA state S₀ = ε-closure({q₀}).
For an unmarked DFA state S and each symbol a in Σ, compute T = ε-closure(move(S, a)). If T is new, add it as a DFA state.
Add a transition S --a--> T. Mark S when all symbols are done. Repeat until no unmarked state remains.
A DFA state is accepting if its set contains at least one NFA accepting state.

blocks.text: The DFA can have at most 2n states for an NFA with n states, because each state is a subset. In practice only reachable subsets appear. LEX uses this recogniser to scan tokens; see 1.9.
Minimisation reduces a DFA to the smallest DFA for the same language. The minimal DFA is unique up to renaming states. Fewer states mean a smaller transition table and a faster lexer.

items: Remove states that cannot be reached from the start state.
Split the remaining states into two groups: accepting states F and non-accepting states Q − F.

For one group, write for each state a tuple with one entry per symbol: the old group that the symbol's transition lands in. States with the same tuple stay together in one new group; states with different tuples go to different new groups. Replace the old group by these new groups. Repeat until no group changes.
Each final group is one state of the minimal DFA. Transitions go to the group of the original target state.

blocks.text: A table-filling method does the same job. Mark pairs of states that are distinguishable. Initially mark a pair if one state is accepting and the other is not. Then mark a pair if some symbol sends them to an already marked pair. Unmarked pairs are equivalent and can be merged.
Do not merge all accepting states automatically. Two accepting states are equivalent only when every symbol sends them to equivalent states. The same rule applies to non-accepting states.

figure.caption: A regular expression is first turned into an NFA. Then ε-closure and subset construction give a DFA. Partition refinement merges equivalent states into the minimal DFA.

spec.title: From regex to DFA
spec.aria: A regular expression becomes an NFA, then a DFA by ε-closure and subset construction, then a minimal DFA by partition refinement.

examples.question: Convert the NFA for a(b|c) to a DFA using subset construction, then minimise the DFA. NFA states are 0 to 5. Start state is 0. Accept states are 3 and 5. Transitions: 0 --a--> 1; 1 --ε--> 2 and 4; 2 --b--> 3; 4 --c--> 5.
steps: Compute the needed ε-closures. ε-closure({0}) = {0}. ε-closure({1}) = {1, 2, 4}. ε-closure({3}) = {3}. ε-closure({5}) = {5}.

Start DFA state A = ε-closure({0}) = {0}. On a: move(A, a) = {1}, so ε-closure({1}) = {1, 2, 4} = B. On b and c: move is empty, so the target is the empty set. We draw a partial DFA and keep the empty dead state E in mind.
From B on b: move(B, b) = {3}, so ε-closure({3}) = {3} = C. From B on c: move(B, c) = {5}, so ε-closure({5}) = {5} = D. From B on a: target is empty.
C and D have no outgoing moves for a, b or c. Their targets are empty.

The DFA states are A = {0}, B = {1,2,4}, C = {3}, D = {5}. Accept states are C and D, because they contain NFA accept states 3 and 5. Transition table: A --a--> B; B --b--> C; B --c--> D; all other moves go to the dead state E.
Minimise. Add dead state E for missing moves. Initial partition: final {C, D} and non-final {A, B, E}. C and D both go to E on a, b, c, so C and D stay together.

In the non-final group, B splits from A and E because on b, A and E go to E (group {A,B,E}) while B goes to C (group {C,D}). First refinement gives groups {A, E}, {B}, {C, D}. Now compare A and E inside {A, E}: on a, A goes to B (group {B}) while E goes to E (group {A, E}); so A and E split. Final groups are {A}, {B}, {C, D}, {E}. Merge C and D into F. Drop E for the partial DFA.
Minimal DFA: A --a--> B; B --b--> F; B --c--> F; F is accepting.
examples.answer: The partial DFA has 4 states A, B, C, D. With the dead state E the complete DFA has 5 states. The minimal partial DFA has 3 states A, B, F.

traps: Take ε-closure before and after every move. Forgetting the closure after move(S, a) misses NFA states that are reachable without reading input.
A subset-construction state is a set of NFA states, not one NFA state. Write braces around it in the transition table.
Minimisation merges only equivalent states. Two accepting states are not automatically equivalent; compare where each symbol sends them.
A DFA is formally complete: every state has a move for every symbol. If you omit the dead state for a drawing, say that the DFA is partial.
The powerset construction can create up to 2<sup>n</sup> states, but only reachable subsets are built. Do not list all subsets by hand.

quiz.a: ε-closure(S) is the set of all NFA states reachable from any state in S by zero or more ε-moves.

quiz.q: Why is an NFA usually easier to build from a regular expression than a DFA?
quiz.a: An NFA allows several moves and ε-moves, so union, concatenation and star can be built with small local changes. A DFA would need those choices resolved immediately.

quiz.q: NFA: start state 0; 0 --a--> 0; 0 --a--> 1; accept state 1. Use subset construction to build the DFA states and transitions.
quiz.a: Start A = {0}. On a, move(A, a) = {0, 1}, so B = {0, 1}. B is accepting. A --a--> B. B --a--> B. The DFA has two states.

quiz.q: Minimise this DFA: states A, B, C; start A is non-final; B and C are final. A --a--> B; A --b--> C; B --a--> B; B --b--> C; C --a--> B; C --b--> C.
quiz.a: B and C are both final and have the same targets for a and b, so merge them into F. Minimal DFA: A --a--> F; A --b--> F; F --a--> F; F --b--> F. Two states.

quiz.q: Two final states in a DFA have the same outgoing symbol labels. Does that prove they are equivalent? Explain.
quiz.a: No. They are equivalent only if each symbol sends them to states that are themselves equivalent. Same labels are not enough; compare the target groups.

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of DFA states produced from an NFA with n states by subset construction?
quiz.a: At most 2<sup>n</sup> DFA states, because each DFA state is a subset of the NFA states.

beyond: Not for the exam. Lexer generators such as LEX build a DFA from token regular expressions and then run it as a table-driven scanner. Modern regular-expression engines often use NFAs or hybrids because NFAs avoid the worst-case subset blow-up. Hopcroft's algorithm and Brzozowski's method are standard ways to minimise automata efficiently. Search next for Thompson construction, Hopcroft DFA minimisation, and powerset construction.
